choices.explanation: Even though we know these legislators are broadly going to be advancing the educational opportunities for women, there's nothing in this window of text that says they're getting rid of "domestic skill education".

choices.text: unaware of the difficulties that the earlier legislators faced when advocating similar legislation
choices.explanation:
We know they're aware of the proposed legislation. We don't know whether or not they're aware of the difficulties it encountered, but presumably they would be.

If you found an old proposed piece of legislation similar to what you're currently proposing, you would presumably find out why the last one failed to pass.

This answer seems to want to fish people into making an unsupported inference that, "If they're trying to push the same agenda that failed a century ago, they must not realize how difficult it's gonna be".

choices.text: concerned with improving educational equality across economic strata as well as between the sexes
choices.explanation:
There's not great support for this, but it's better than any other choice.

We know they were helping educational equality for women by "founding public secondary schools for women" (and compulsory attendance also meant that women couldn't be pulled out of school early to learn domestic stuff at home).

The support for better equality across economic strata (i.e. working class, middle class, upper class) is that they proposed "abolishing fees" for education.

Fees for schooling would presumably price out some poorer citizens, but if you abolish fees than you help to equalize educational access.

choices.text: more open to political compromise than were the legislators who introduced the previous proposals for reform
choices.explanation:
We have no ammunition for making that comparison. This seems to invite the illicit inference that "if THEY were able to get THEIRS passed, then these legislators must have been more willing to compromise".

Maybe. But it's at least as likely that the difference between the failure of these reforms to pass the first time and the successful passage 100 years later is simply that the culture had changed over the course of 100 years to be more receptive to / demanding of these reforms.

choices.text: more inclined to give religious authorities a role in education than were the legislators who introduced the previous proposals for reform
choices.tag: No Support: "more inclined to give religion role"
choices.explanation: We can't judge this comparison, since our snippet of text on the 1880s legislators includes no information about what role religious authorities would / wouldn't be playing.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Prephrase
explanationBlocks.body:
If we think back to our passage map, we had ingredients such as this:
- some people think the Revolution missed their chance to do something good
- author says "these two reforms were attempts at good, and here's a description of what each one was"
- author says "it's understandable why they failed to pass, and they weren't useless. They actually helped the eventual similar stuff to pass 100 years later"

The "shortcut" on Organization problems can be to check on the last ingredient first, since many of these answers start off reasonably matching but diverge along the way.

choices.text: Education in France during one historical period is described; two proposals that attempted to reform the educational system are presented; inconsistencies within each proposal are identified and lamented.
choices.explanation: The last paragraph had nothing to do with the author finding contradictions (inconsistencies) within these proposals and complaining about them.

choices.text: The movement toward gender equality in France during one historical period is discussed; two proposals for educational reform are presented; the differences between the proposals and the educational system of that era are outlined.
choices.explanation:
The proposals came at the end of the 1700s. According to this answer, the last paragraph is outlining differences between the proposals and the educational system of the late 1700s.

But the last paragraph is talking about how reform that passed in the late 1800s is similar to (and somewhat reliant upon) the two proposals.

choices.text: The traditional nature of French education for women is described; proposed breaks with tradition are discussed, followed by a discussion of why eventual change required less of a break with tradition.
choices.explanation:
The first paragraph doesn't quite describe the traditional nature of French education for women. it says that in the 1800s, they were still educating women according to long established models, but there's no additional detail or description.

And the last paragraph isn't saying that when reforms ultimately passed, it was *not* a break with this tradition. It's saying that the reforms managed to pass in part because the two "radical" proposals that came out after the Revolution helped the people in 1880 argue that they weren't being totally crazy; their bold new ideas had precedent in post-Revolutionary thinking.

choices.text: The egalitarian aims in France during one historical period are presented; proposals that foreshadowed eventual reform are described; the initial characterization of the aims is modified.
choices.explanation: The last paragraph does not modify how it characterized the aims of post-Revolution France. To the contrary, it says that legislators were successful in passing the reform proposals in part by showing how they aligned with the egalitarian aims of post-Revolution France.

choices.text: The nature of education for women in France during one historical period is described; proposals for educational reform are presented; the relationship between the proposals and eventual reform is indicated.
choices.explanation: 1st paragraph describes how the nature of education for women in most of 1800s France was similar to that of its traditional past. 2nd paragraph breaks down the two proposed educational reforms. 3rd paragraph shows how those proposals actually kinda helped in the passing of the eventual reform.

questions.prompt: Suppose that two proposals were put forward by lawmakers concerning housing reform today. Which one of the following pairs of proposals is most closely analogous to the pair of proposals discussed in the second paragraph of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Prephrase
explanationBlocks.body:
It's hard to guess what aspects of the two proposals in the passage the answer choice will reinforce: better access for women? less focus on religion? available for everyone? got rejected because of immense cultural and political obstacles?

Once we start peeking at how the answers are structured, we see that we need to draw a contrast between the two proposals. What was their salient difference?

1st one - better access for women / teachers from both sexes / but women would only be in school until age 8

2nd one - more comprehensive / girls and boys in same classrooms

I'd primarily be looking for the 2nd one to be a more comprehensive attempt at equality.

choices.text: "Housing should be made available to all" and "Real estate practices should be nondiscriminatory"
choices.explanation:
We can match the first one, since the first proposal said "since education is a common good, instruction *should be available to everyone*.

We can match the second one, since the second proposal said "*equal education for women and men*", and we know it was aimed at getting rid of the discriminatory practice of siphoning out women around age 8 to learn domestic stuff.

choices.text: "Housing should be made available to all" and "The quality of housing should be improved"
choices.explanation:
We can match up the first part as we did in choice (A), since they're identical. But there isn't a strong line reference match for *improving quality* when it comes to the 2nd proposal.

Neither "equaled for women and men" nor "coed schools" are an obvious match for "improved quality".

choices.text: "There should be housing for all who can pay" and "Housing should be of uniform quality"
choices.explanation:
Although the 2nd proposal's call for "equal education for women and men" matches decently with *uniform* quality, the 1st proposal doesn't contain anything relating to who can / can't pay for education.

In fact, since the 1st proposal calls for public school throughout the country, it seems like it's suggesting education for all, not just for all who can pay.

choices.text: "The quality of housing should be improved" and "Real estate practices should be nondiscriminatory"
choices.explanation:
The 2nd one works as it does in the correct answer (A), but it's hard to find any keywords that sound like *improved* quality to match up with the 1st.

Even though we probably think of it as an improvement that they were going to have teachers of both sexes, deemphasize the primarily religious education, and make sure women had access to school (until age 8 at least), none of those are synonymous with an "improved quality" of education.

choices.text: "Low-cost housing should be constructed" and "Housing should be of uniform quality"
choices.explanation:
The 2nd ingredient matches fine with the idea of "equal education for women and men", but it's hard to find a good match for "construct low-cost education" in the 1st proposal.

We'd have to assume that replacing religious with reformed curricula, or offering education to both sexes, or hiring teachers of both sexes, or establishing public schools for women and men is "constructing low-cost housing".

The last ingredient seems the best match, since establishing and constructing are similar. Is calling for low-cost housing similar to calling for public school? Kinda. They're both aimed at the non-rich segment of society.

This just seems to lose to (A) because given that (A) had a smattering of proposals, this answer will probably want us to prioritize the headline of each proposal. Building public schools ("low-cost" education) would be done for both boys and girls.

But the main reason we're talking about these two proposals is their effect on the education for women, so the part of the first proposal that is most salient to women ("More importantly, ....") is the idea that "school should be offered to girls, too".

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the second of the two proposals discussed was distinctive because it asserted that

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text / Prephrase
explanationBlocks.body:
In the end of the 2nd paragraph it says, "the second proposal took a more comprehensive approach". That must be the difference they're testing. How was it more comprehensive / thorough than the first one?

The next thought is that it *advocated for equal education for women and men*, so did the first one not do that?

The first one says that *"instruction should be available to everyone",* but I guess there's a difference between "everyone can have an apple" and "all apples are equal". The unequal part of the first proposal was that girls, unlike boys, had to leave school at age 8 to learn domestic skills.

The passage also says that the second proposal was "*the only* proposal" to call for coed schools.

choices.text: everyone should both learn and teach
choices.explanation: "Teachers will be drawn from both sexes" was a provision of the 1st proposal.

choices.text: males and females should go to the same schools
choices.explanation:
The 2nd was *the only* one that called for coed schools (coed = boys and girls attend the same school).

If we didn't know what "coed" meant, then we're pretty much screwed here.

choices.text: education should involve lifelong learning
choices.explanation: If there's anything that matches this, it's the "yank girls out at age 8 so that they can learn *the skills necessary for domestic life and for the raising of families*." from the first proposal.

choices.text: religious schools should be abolished
choices.explanation: "Abolished" is super strong, and neither proposal says anything like outlawing religious schools.

choices.text: education for girls should be both public and secular
choices.explanation: Both proposals tolerate religion but deemphasize it. The first proposal is replacing mostly religious education with reformed curricula. The second proposal is acting as a bulwark against the traditional roles enforced by religious tradition.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, the fact that the proposed reforms were introduced shortly after the French Revolution most clearly suggests that the proposals

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
The last sentence of the first paragraph is where we learn that these proposals came out shortly after the French Revolution, and it begins with "However", so the function of this sentence is evidently to counter the idea in the previous sentence.

Since the previous sentence is saying, "Given that the Revolution had aims at making society more equal and less religious (egalitarian and secular)", it would be a missed opportunity to have not reformed schooling for women in those directions at that point.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Our author is saying, "They tried! Right after the Revolution they had some reforms that were trying to improve education for women in more egalitarian and secular ways."

choices.text: were a reaction to the excesses of the new government
choices.explanation: They were in line with the Revolution, which was in reaction to the former government.

choices.text: had their roots in a belief in the power of education
choices.tag: No Support: "rooted in power of ed belief"
choices.explanation: There's nothing we can point to at the end of the first paragraph that makes it seem like "shortly after Revolution = based in the power of education"

choices.text: had vast popular support within French society
choices.explanation: We learn later that these proposals were not passed due to the headwinds of cultural and political obstacles. So even though these proposals were in keeping with the spirit of the Revolution, we don't have textual support for *vast popular support* and we even have what seems to be counterevidence to that idea.

choices.text: treated education for women as a prerequisite to the implementation of other reforms
choices.explanation:
Since these proposals weren't passed, it would be surprising to characterize them as the "first thing that needs to be done, before we implement any other reforms".

The passage is giving off the opposite gist, that after the Revolution when other things were being reformed it seems like a missed opportunity that education was *not* reformed.

choices.text: were influenced by egalitarian ideals
choices.explanation:
Yes, this not only reinforces what it says in the same sentence, that these "two in particular were, to a great extent, egalitarian", but it also reinforces the connection to the previous sentence.

The fact that these proposals came right after the Revolution shows, the author argues, that the post-Revolutionary spirit of egalitarianism and secularism *did* try to have an effect on education.

questions.prompt: The author would most likely describe the proposals mentioned in the passage with which one of the following statements?

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text / Prephrase
explanationBlocks.body:
We need to think about where the author expressed her view on these proposals. We know she brings them up in defense of the idea that it wasn't quite a *missed opportunity* that there was no educational reform following the Revolution. *They tried!*

We also hear her disappointment with the two proposals, at the end of first paragraph, by saying "in other ways, though, this 2nd one was still kinda crappy in terms of relegating women to domestic identities".

And the final paragraph puts a positive spin on the proposals, saying that they were actually useful precedents to have that facilitated the passage of the eventual reform.

choices.text: They espoused reforms that were very modest by the standards of the day.
choices.explanation: Beginning of the 3rd paragraph would go against this. He thinks there were "immense cultural and political obstacles to egalitarianism at the time".

choices.text: They were fundamentally unethical due to their incomplete view of equality.
choices.explanation: Our author seems unimpressed with certain traditional ideas retained in the proposals, but overall she's presenting them as though they were an honorable attempt at a step forward.

choices.text: They were well-meaning attempts to do as much as was feasible at the time.
choices.explanation: This captures the overall positivity ("they *tried* to make things better, but they were up against strong forces, and even the attempt was useful when it came to passing the eventual reform") as well as the tinge of resigned realism (they did both continue to define women in terms of domestic roles).

choices.text: They were reasonable, and it is difficult to understand why they failed.
choices.explanation: The beginning of the 3rd paragraph shows that the author is not surprised that they initially failed, so she finds their failure understandable.

choices.text: They were not adopted because their aims were not fully comprehensive.
choices.explanation: She thinks they weren't adapted because they were too radical for their time, not because they weren't radical enough (as this answer choice implies).
